Why would anyone be blowing on a cartridge that was working?

Dust was a problem, but the biggest problem was the hinge inside the machine which was often faulty. Nintendo of America decided to forgo the traditional cartridge slot of the Atari and Famicom design for something more akin to a VCR to make it appear more "grown up" and less like a normal console, to avoid the stigma of video games after the crash of '83. So when the hinge played up and the connector and socket didn't align correctly, people ended up blowing on them thinking dust was the problem. And it frequently was, due to the NES (not the Famicom) design, but that was only one of three main causes of NES games not loading correctly (dust, hinge/connectors, corrosion). The later top-loading NES redesign (with the amazing dogbone controller) fixed two of those issues, but games still frequently didn't work due to corrosion, often caused by blowing on them. In fact the cartridges themselves have a warning label to tell you not to blow on them for this very reason.

I've also seen pushing the game in the absolutely minimum amount work, or pushing it to the right or left or kinda diagonal, or sticking another game in on top of it after it was pushed down work. The point was just to try to get the whichever connector wasn't working into a minutely different position or to apply a little bit more pressure. People had slightly different techniques because it was pretty clear that the connection was somehow bad and that if you could just get the connectors to touch in in some slightly different way, it would work. I don't remember thinking about the moisture factor of blowing in the cartridge or console, but I wouldn't be surprised if I had considered it, because the factors are pretty elementary, even at a pretty young age. Kids breath on windows and mirrors, and they that a hair dryer or toaster in the bathtub will kill ya. Now I almost do remember maybe also trying breathing slower warmer air onto the cartridge, but I'm not sure whether I'm just imaging. It's a reasonable thing I may have tried and it may have sometimes worked. Yeah, the more I try to correctly remember, I think it probably was one of the techniques I used. At some point I think there were also specialized cleaning products. I'm not sure I ever had those, but they may have explained the possibility of moisture corrosion from water, although even that is a pretty basic concept at a fairly young age since kids know about metal rusting, even if they don't know rust being related to iron or how other metals corrode.
